title: Viscum album

{{Short description|Species of flowering plant}} {{Speciesbox |image = Viscum album 2026 G1.jpg |image_caption = Evergreen ''Viscum album''
in winter, growing on ''[[Populus tremula]]'' | status = LC | status_system = IUCN3.1 | status_ref = {{cite iucn |author=Chappuis, E. |date=2014 |title=Viscum album (Europe assessment) |volume=2014 |article-number=e.T203473A2766017 |access-date=11 October 2023}} |genus = Viscum |species = album |authority = [[Carl Linnaeus|L.]] }} [[File:Krijtlandpad – Viscum album in the Netherlands (cropped).jpg|thumb|225px|''Viscum album'' growing on winter dormant trees in the Netherlands]] '''''Viscum album''''' is a species of [[mistletoe]] in the family [[Santalaceae]], commonly called '''European mistletoe''', '''common mistletoe''', or simply '''mistletoe''' ([[Old English]] ''mistle'').{{cite journal |last=Zuber|first=Doris |title=Biological flora of Central Europe: Viscum album L. |journal=Flora: Morphology, Distribution, Functional Ecology of Plants |publisher=[[Elsevier]] BV |volume=199 |issue=3 |year=2004 |issn=0367-2530 |doi=10.1078/0367-2530-00147 |pages=181–203 |bibcode=2004FMDFE.199..181Z}} It is native to [[Europe]], as well as western and southern [[Asia]].{{cite journal |last1=O'Neill|first1=A. R. |last2=Rana|first2=S. K. | date=2019 |title=An ethnobotanical analysis of parasitic plants (Parijibi) in the Nepal Himalaya |journal=[[BioMed Central|Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine]] |volume=12 |issue=14 |page=14 |doi=10.1186/s13002-016-0086-y |pmid=26912113 |pmc=4765049 |doi-access=free}} ''V. album'' is found only rarely in [[North America]], as an [[introduced species]]. ''Viscum album'' is a [[hemiparasite]] on several species of trees, from which it draws water and nutrients. It has a significant role in European mythology, legends, and customs. In modern times, it is commonly featured among [[Christmas]] decorations and symbology. In North America its cultural roles are usually fulfilled by the similar native species, ''[[Phoradendron leucarpum]]''. Long used in alternative medicine traditions without any academic basis, mistletoe now is under study for pharmaceutical uses in modern medicine. == Description == It is a [[parasitic plant|hemi-parasitic]] evergreen [[shrub]], which grows on the stems of other trees. The plant contains a [[haustorium]] that connects it to the host tree by connecting the xylem and phloem of the mistletoe to that of the host tree, which allows it to receive nutrients and water.{{Cite journal |last1=Krasylenko |first1=Yuliya |last2=Sosnovsky |first2=Yevhen |last3=Atamas |first3=Natalia |last4=Popov |first4=Grigory |last5=Leonenko |first5=Volodymyr |last6=Janošíková |first6=Kateřina |last7=Sytschak |first7=Nadiya |last8=Rydlo |first8=Karol |last9=Sytnyk |first9=Dmytro |date=September 2020 |title=The European mistletoe (Viscum album L.): distribution, host range, biotic interactions, and management worldwide with special emphasis on Ukraine |url=http://www.nrcresearchpress.com/doi/10.1139/cjb-2020-0037 |journal=Botany |language=en |volume=98 |issue=9 |pages=499–516 |doi=10.1139/cjb-2020-0037 |issn=1916-2790|url-access=subscription |hdl=1807/101820 |hdl-access=free }} It has stems {{convert|30|-|100|cm|in}} long with dichotomous branching. The [[leaf|leaves]] are in opposite pairs, strap-shaped, entire, leathery textured, {{convert|2|-|8|cm|in}} long, {{convert|0.8|-|2.5|cm|in}} broad and are a yellowish-green in colour. This species is [[dioecious]] and the insect-pollinated [[flower]]s are inconspicuous, yellowish-green, {{convert|2|-|3|mm|in}} diameter. The [[fruit]] is a white or yellow [[Berry (botany)|berry]], and except for very rarely, containing one [[seed]] embedded in the very sticky, glutinous fruit pulp. It is commonly found in the crowns of broad-leaved trees, particularly [[apple]], [[Tilia|lime]] (linden), [[Crataegus monogyna|hawthorn]], and [[Populus|poplar]].{{cite web | last=Broadmeadow | first=Mark | title=ISSUE 9 – Spring/Summer 2005 | website=Tree News Magazine | url=http://www.treenews.org.uk/latest/index.php | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060103200008/http://www.treenews.org.uk/latest/index.php | archive-date=2006-01-03 }} European mistletoe is the only multicellular organism known to lack a functioning [[respiratory complex I]] in its [[electron transport chain]], a protein that is essential for the creation of useful energy for its cells.{{Cite web|title=Mistletoe is missing the machinery to make energy|url=https://www.science.org/content/article/mistletoe-missing-machinery-make-energy|access-date=2022-02-08|website=www.science.org|language=en}} It is believed to survive by obtaining [[adenosine triphosphate]] and energy-rich compounds from its host as well as reorganizing its other respiratory complexes and slowing its growth and energy requirements.{{Cite journal|last1=Fonseca-Pereira|first1=Paula da|last2=Silva|first2=Willian Batista|last3=Araújo|first3=Wagner L.|last4=Nunes-Nesi|first4=Adriano|date=2018-10-01|title=How Does European Mistletoe Survive Without Complex I?|url=https://www.cell.com/trends/plant-science/abstract/S1360-1385(18)30164-X|journal=Trends in Plant Science|language=English|volume=23|issue=10|pages=847–850|doi=10.1016/j.tplants.2018.07.008|issn=1360-1385|pmid=30097375|bibcode=2018TPS....23..847D |s2cid=51956904 |url-access=subscription}} == Classification == The mistletoe was one of the many species originally described by the Swedish scientist [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]]. Its species name is the [[Latin]] adjective {{Lang|la|albus}}, "white". It and the other members of the genus ''[[Viscum]]'' were originally classified in the mistletoe family [[Viscaceae]], but this family has since been reclassified into the larger family [[Santalaceae]]. === Subspecies === Several [[subspecies]] are commonly accepted.{{cite web | title=Flora Europaea Search Results = Viscum album | website=Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh | url=https://websites.rbge.org.uk/cgi-bin/nph-readbtree.pl/feout?FAMILY_XREF=&GENUS_XREF=Viscum&SPECIES_XREF=album&TAXON_NAME_XREF=&RANK= | access-date=2022-08-25}}{{cite web | title=Viscum album Linnaeus subsp. meridianum | website=Flora of China @ efloras.org | url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=242414826 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303193026/http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=242414826 | archive-date=2016-03-03 | url-status=live}}{{cite book |last=Bean |first=W. J. |year=1980 |title=Trees and Shrubs Hardy in the British Isles |edition=8th |volume=4 |pages=725–726 |publisher=J. Murray |isbn=0-7195-2428-8}}{{cite book | last1=Blamey | first1=Marjorie | last2=Grey-Wilson | first2=Christopher | title=The illustrated flora of Britain and northern Europe | publisher=Hodder & Stoughton | publication-place=London | date=1989 | isbn=0-340-40170-2 | oclc=41355268}} They differ in fruit colour, leaf shape and size, and most obviously in the host trees used. *''Viscum album'' subsp. '''''abietis''''' (Wiesb.) Abromeit. [[Central Europe]]. Fruit white; leaves up to {{convert|8|cm|in}}. On ''[[fir|Abies]]''. *''Viscum album'' subsp. '''''album'''''. Europe, [[southwest Asia]] east to [[Nepal]]. Fruit white; leaves {{convert|3|-|5|cm|in}}. On ''[[Malus]]'', ''[[Populus]]'', ''[[Tilia]]'', and less often on numerous other species, including (rarely) ''[[oak|Quercus]]''. *''Viscum album'' subsp. '''''austriacum''''' (Wiesb.) Vollmann. Fruit yellow; leaves {{convert|2|-|4|cm}}. Central Europe. On ''[[larch|Larix]]'', ''[[pine|Pinus]]'', ''[[spruce|Picea]]''. *''Viscum album'' subsp. '''''meridianum''''' (Danser) D.G.Long. [[Southeast Asia]]. Fruit yellow; leaves {{convert|3|-|5|cm|in}}. On ''[[maple|Acer]]'', ''[[hornbeam|Carpinus]]'', ''[[walnut|Juglans]]'', ''[[Prunus]]'', ''[[Sorbus]]''. *''Viscum album'' subsp. '''''creticum''''' has recently been described from eastern [[Crete]].{{cite journal | last1=Böhling | first1=Niels | last2=Greuter | first2=Werner | last3=Raus | first3=Thomas | last4=Snogerup | first4=Britt | last5=Snogerup | first5=Sven | last6=Snogerup | first6=b Sven | title=Notes on the Cretan mistletoe, Viscum album subsp. creticum subsp. nova (Loranthaceae/Viscaceae) | journal=Israel Journal of Plant Sciences | publisher=Laser Pages Publishing Ltd. | volume=50 | issue=1 | date=2002-01-01 | issn=0792-9978 | doi=10.1560/rrj4-hu15-8bfm-wauk |pages=77–84| doi-broken-date=12 July 2025 }} Fruit white; leaves short. On ''[[Turkish Pine|Pinus brutia]]''. *''Viscum album'' subsp. '''''coloratum''''' Kom. is treated by the ''[[Flora of China (series)|Flora of China]]'' as a distinct species ''[[Viscum coloratum]]'' (Kom) Nakai. == Distribution and habitat == {{Empty section|date=October 2024}} == Genetics == The European mistletoe has one of the largest [[genome]]s of all organisms, at about 90 billion base pairs (compared to ~3 billion bp in the [[human genome]]). It encodes 39,092 distinct [[open reading frame]]s encoding 32,064 [[protein]]s.{{Cite journal |last1=Schröder |first1=Lucie |last2=Hohnjec |first2=Natalija |last3=Senkler |first3=Michael |last4=Senkler |first4=Jennifer |last5=Küster |first5=Helge |last6=Braun |first6=Hans-Peter |date=January 2022 |title=The gene space of European mistletoe (Viscum album) |journal=The Plant Journal |language=en |volume=109 |issue=1 |pages=278–294 |doi=10.1111/tpj.15558 |issn=0960-7412|doi-access=free |pmid=34713513 |bibcode=2022PlJ...109..278S }} == Toxicity == {{Globalize|section|America|date=March 2025}} If ingested in a concentrated form, such as a herbal tea infusion, European mistletoe is potentially fatal. Otherwise, people have been known to become seriously ill from eating the berries.{{cite web | title=Is mistletoe poisonous? | website=Poison Control | url=https://www.poison.org/articles/mistletoe}} The toxic [[lectin]] [[viscumin]] has been isolated from ''Viscum album''.{{cite journal |vauthors=Olsnes S, Stirpe F, Sandvig K, Pihl A |title=Isolation and characterization of viscumin, a toxic lectin from Viscum album L. (mistletoe) |journal=The Journal of Biological Chemistry |volume=257 |issue=22 |pages=13263–70 |date=November 1982 |doi=10.1016/S0021-9258(18)33440-9 |pmid=7142144 |doi-access=free }} Viscumin is a cytotoxic protein ([[ribosome inactivating protein]], or RIP) that binds to [[galactose]] residues of cell surface [[glycoprotein]]s and may be internalised by [[endocytosis]].{{cite journal |vauthors=Stirpe F, Sandvig K, Olsnes S, Pihl A |title=Action of viscumin, a toxic lectin from mistletoe, on cells in culture |journal=The Journal of Biological Chemistry |volume=257 |issue=22 |pages=13271–7 |date=November 1982 |doi=10.1016/S0021-9258(18)33441-0 |pmid=7142145 |doi-access=free }} Viscumin strongly inhibits protein synthesis by inactivating the 60 S ribosomal subunit. The structure of this protein is very similar to other RIPs, showing the most resemblance to [[ricin]] and [[abrin]]. Some birds have immunity to the toxin and enjoy the berries, especially the [[mistle thrush]] that is so named because mistletoe is their favourite food. Birds are especially important in distributing the seeds of the plant to new locations in the trees in which it will grow. == Cultural folklore and mythology == [[File:AEneas finds the golden bough Frontispieace Leaves from the Golden Bough.jpg|thumb|345x345px|Roman ancestor Aeneas finds the Golden Bough.]] European mistletoe features in many myths and legends, from early written sources into the modern period. In cultures across pre-Christian Europe, mistletoe was often seen as a representation of divine male essence (and thus romance, fertility, and vitality).{{Cite Q|Q119858256}} === Ancient Greek and Roman === Mistletoe figured prominently in [[Greek mythology]], and is believed to be the [[The Golden Bough (mythology)|Golden Bough]] of [[Aeneas]], ancestor of the [[Ancient Rome|Romans]].Virgil (19 BCE) The Aeneid In Ancient Greek mythology, mistletoe was used by heroes to access the underworld.{{cite web |last=Bonham |first=Emma |date=2015-12-01 |title=Mistletoe: meaning, mythology and magic |url=https://www.woodlandtrust.org.uk/blog/2015/12/mistletoe/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181209124006/https://www.woodlandtrust.org.uk/blog/2015/12/mistletoe/ |archive-date=2018-12-09 |website=woodlandtrust.org.uk}} The [[Roman Empire|Romans]] associated mistletoe with peace, love, and understanding. They hung mistletoe over doorways to protect the household.{{cite web |last=Bell |first=Bethan |date=2013-12-10 |title=Tenbury Wells: Centuries-old romance with mistletoe |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-england-hereford-worcester-24987280 |website=BBC News}} === Celtic === [[File:Motte Druide coupant le gui au 6e jour de la lune.jpg|thumb|318x318px|The oak and mistletoe ritual depicted by [[Henri-Paul Motte]] (1900)]] [[Pliny the Elder]] makes an account in his [[Natural History (Pliny)|''Natural History'']] about the [[Celts|Celtic]] religious [[Ritual of oak and mistletoe]], in which [[Druid|druids]] would climb [[oak]] trees to cut down the mistletoe growing on it where it would then be turned into an elixir said to cure infertility and the effects of poison {{Cquote | quote = "We should not omit to mention the great admiration that the Gauls have for it as well. The druids – that is what they call their magicians – hold nothing more sacred than the mistletoe and a tree on which it is growing, provided it is [[Quercus robur|a hard-timbered oak]] .... Mistletoe is rare and when found it is gathered with great ceremony, and particularly on the [[lunar phase|sixth day of the moon]].... Hailing the moon in a native word that means 'healing all things,' they prepare a ritual sacrifice and banquet beneath a tree and bring up two white bulls, whose horns are bound for the first time on this occasion. A priest arrayed in white vestments climbs the tree and, with a golden sickle, cuts down the mistletoe, which is caught in a white cloak. Then finally they kill the victims, praying to a god to render his gift propitious to those on whom he has bestowed it. They believe that mistletoe given in drink will impart fertility to any animal that is barren and that it is an antidote to all poisons." | author = Pliny the Elder | source = {{cite book | last = Pliny the Elder | title = Natural History, Book 16, Chapter 95 | translator = John Bostock & H.T. Riley | publisher = H. G. Bohn | year = 1855 | url = https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus:text:1999.02.0137:book=16:chapter=95 | access-date = 30 December 2025 }} }} === Germanic === [[File:Each arrow overshot his head by Elmer Boyd Smith.jpg|thumb|''Each arrow overshot his head'' (1902) by [[Elmer Boyd Smith]], depicts the blind god [[Höðr]] shooting his brother, the god [[Baldr]], with a mistletoe arrow]] "Things" are governing assemblies or forums in early Germanic society and similar gatherings appear in German mythology and historical accounts of the religious and social practices of the culture. Mistletoe appears in the thirteenth century ''[[Prose Edda]]'' account of German traditions. One account relates that the goddess [[Frigg]] required that everything swear an oath not to hurt her son [[Baldr]], except for mistletoe, because "it seemed too young" to be a threat to her son. At [[Thing (assembly)|thing]] gatherings of deities that followed, other deities began to have fun by shooting at him, or hurling stones, without him being injured at all. At one gathering however, [[Loki]], wishing Baldr dead, tricked the blind god [[Höðr]] who was Baldr's brother, into throwing mistletoe at Baldr, killing him.{{cite book |translator-last=Faulkes |translator-first=Anthony |year=1995 |title=[[Edda]] |pages=48–49 |publisher=[[Everyman's Library|Everyman]] |isbn=0-460-87616-3}} In another version of the myth in {{Lang|la|[[Gesta Danorum]]}}, Baldr and Höðr are rival suitors for [[Nanna (Norse deity)|Nanna]], and Höðr kills Baldr with a sword named [[Mistilteinn]] ([[Old Norse]] "mistletoe").{{cite book |author=[[Saxo Grammaticus]] |editor=[[Hilda Ellis Davidson]] |translator=Peter Fisher |date=17 January 2008 |title=Saxo Grammaticus: The History of the Danes, Books I-IX |edition=revised |location=Woodbridge, Suffolk, UK & Rochester, NY |publisher=[[Boydell & Brewer]] |isbn=978-0-85991-502-1}} Additionally, a sword by the same name also appears in [[Hervarar saga ok Heiðreks]] and [[Hrómundar saga Gripssonar]].{{cite book |last1=Simek |first1=Rudolf |title=Dictionary of northern mythology |date=1993 |publisher=D.S. Brewer |location=Cambridge [England] |isbn=978-0-85991-513-7}} === Christian === [[File:Mistletoe Postcard 1900.jpg|thumb|Mistletoe postcard, circa 1900]] When Christianity became widespread in Europe after the third century AD, the ancient religious or mystical respect for the mistletoe plant was absorbed only as a cultural tradition. In some way that is not presently understood, this may have led to the widespread custom of [[kissing]] under the mistletoe plant during the Christmas season. The earliest documented evidence of the tradition of kissing under the mistletoe dates from sixteenth century England, a custom that was apparently very popular at that time. [[Winston Graham]] reports a Cornish tradition that mistletoe was originally a fine tree from which the wood of the [[Christian Cross|Cross]] was made, but afterward it was condemned to live on only as a parasite.{{Cite book|title= Bella Poldark |last=Graham|first=Winston|publisher=Macmillan|year=2002 |chapter= Chapter 6 }} Mistletoe is commonly used as a [[Christmas decoration]], although such use was rarely alluded to until the eighteenth century.{{cite journal | last=Drury | first=Susan | title=Customs and Beliefs Associated with Christmas Evergreens: A Preliminary Survey | journal=Folklore | publisher=Informa UK Limited | volume=98 | issue=2 | year=1987 | issn=0015-587X | doi=10.1080/0015587x.1987.9716413 | pages=194–199}} According to custom, the mistletoe must not touch the ground between its cutting and its removal as the last of Christmas greens at [[Candlemas]]. It may remain hanging throughout the year, often to preserve the house from [[lightning]] or fire, until it is replaced the following Christmas Eve.{{cite web | last=Peffley | first=Ellen | title=The history and not-so-romantic truth about mistletoe | website=Lubbock Avalanche-Journal | date=2013-12-25 | url=https://www.lubbockonline.com/story/lifestyle/columns/2013/12/25/peffley-history-and-not-so-romantic-truth-about-mistletoe/15061569007/}} This tradition has spread throughout the English-speaking world, but is largely unknown in the rest of Europe. (The similar native species ''[[Phoradendron leucarpum]]'' is used in [[North America]] in lieu of the European ''Viscum album''.) According to an old Christmas custom, a man and a woman who meet under a hanging of mistletoe were obliged to [[kiss]]. The custom may be of [[Scandinavia]]n origin.E. Cobham Brewer, ''Dictionary of Phrase and Fable'' 1898, ''s.v. "Kissing under the mistletoe" relates the custom to the death of Baldr, without authority.'' It was alluded to as common practice in 1808In a newspaper advertisement for shaving products:'THE KISS UNDER THE MISSELTOE. Under the misseltoe the maid was led/Altho' she cried, No, she held up her head/To obtain a kiss: a sigh was heard./The reason why - Tom rubbed her with his beard' ''The Times'' (London, England), 13 October 1808; p.4 and described in 1820 by American author [[Washington Irving]] in his ''[[The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent.]]'': {{blockquote|The mistletoe is still hung up in farm-houses and kitchens at Christmas, and the young men have the privilege of kissing the girls under it, plucking each time a berry from the bush. When the berries are all plucked the privilege ceases.{{cite book | last=Irving | first=Washington | title=The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent | publisher=G. P. Putnam | series=Works of Washington Irving | year=1849 | chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=06YhAAAAMAAJ&pg=PA254 | page=254 |chapter=Christmas Eve}}}} In Germany, the Christmas tradition is that people who kiss under mistletoe will have an enduring love or are bound to marry one another.{{cite news |url=https://www.zeit.de/wissen/2009-11/adventskalender-mistel |title=Warum küsst man sich unter dem Mistelzweig? |language=de |newspaper=Die Zeit|date=30 November 2015 |last1=Nitzsche |first1=Richard }} === Other traditions === Every year, the UK town of [[Tenbury Wells]] holds a mistletoe festival and crowns a 'Mistletoe Queen'. Mistletoe is the [[County flowers of the United Kingdom|county flower]] of [[Herefordshire]]. It was voted such in 2002, following a poll by the wild plant conservation charity [[Plantlife]].{{cite web | title=Mistletoe | website=Plantlife | url=https://www.plantlife.org.uk/uk/discover-wild-plants-nature/plant-fungi-species/mistletoe | access-date=2022-08-26 | archive-date=2022-12-06 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221206175825/https://www.plantlife.org.uk/uk/discover-wild-plants-nature/plant-fungi-species/mistletoe }} == Contemporary uses == === Lexicographic === The Latin word {{Langx|la|viscum|lit=mistletoe, birdlime|label=none}} is the source of ''viscous''.{{cite web |last1=Harper |first1=Douglas |title=viscous {{!}} Origin and meaning of viscous by Online Etymology Dictionary |url=https://www.etymonline.com/word/viscous#etymonline_v_7831 |website=www.etymonline.com |access-date=22 May 2021 |language=en}} === Bird trapping === The sticky juice of mistletoe berries was used to make [[birdlime]], an [[adhesive]] to [[animal trapping#glue traps|trap]] small animals or birds.{{cite book | last=Johnson | first=T.B. | title=The Sportsman's Cyclopaedia | publisher=Henry G. Bohn | year=1848 | url=https://archive.org/details/sportsmanscyclop00john/page/56 | page=56}} === Flavoring === Mistletoe is an ingredient of ''[[biska]]'', a [[pomace brandy]]-based liquor made in [[Istria]].{{cite news | last = Rushby | first = Kevin | title = Cres, Croatia: island of ghosts and vultures | newspaper = The Guardian | date = 20 August 2016 | url = https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2016/aug/20/cres-island-croatia-road-trip | access-date = 27 December 2017 }} === Medicinal === {{Further|Anthroposophic medicine#Mistletoe treatment for cancer}} Mistletoe leaves and young twigs are used by herbalists and preparations made from them are popular in Europe, especially in [[Germany]], for attempting to treat circulatory and respiratory system problems.{{cite journal | last1=Ernst | first1=Eduard | last2=Schmidt | first2=Katja | last3=Steuer-Vogt | first3=Miriam Katharina | title=Mistletoe for cancer? A systematic review of randomised clinical trials | journal=International Journal of Cancer | publisher=Wiley | volume=107 | issue=2 | date=2003-08-26 | issn=0020-7136 | pmid=12949804 | doi=10.1002/ijc.11386 | pages=262–267| s2cid=46016570 | doi-access=free }}{{cite web | title=Mistletoe | website=drugdigest.org| url=http://www.drugdigest.org/DD/PrintablePages/herbMonograph/0,11475,4043,00.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080719181505/http://www.drugdigest.org/DD/PrintablePages/herbMonograph/0,11475,4043,00.html | archive-date=2008-07-19 | url-status=unfit}}{{cite web | title=A Modern Herbal - Mistletoe | website=Botanical.com | url=http://www.botanical.com/botanical/mgmh/m/mistle40.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160821231036/http://www.botanical.com/botanical/mgmh/m/mistle40.html | archive-date=2016-08-21 | url-status=live}} Use of mistletoe extract in the treatment of cancer originated with [[Rudolf Steiner]], the founder of [[Anthroposophy]].{{cite journal|title=European and Oriental mistletoe: From mythology to contemporary integrative cancer care|journal=European Journal of Integrative Medicine|date=September 2011 |volume=3 |issue=3 |pages=e133–e137 |doi=10.1016/j.eujim.2011.05.052 |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1876382011001181 |last1=Lev |first1=Efraim |last2=Ephraim |first2=Marco |last3=Ben-Arye |first3=Eran |url-access=subscription }} === Scientific research === Although [[in vitro|laboratory]] and [[in vivo|animal]] experiments have suggested that mistletoe extract may affect the [[immune system]] and be able to kill some kinds of cancer cells, as of 2024, there is little [[evidence-based medicine|evidence]] of its benefit to people with cancer.{{cite web |url=http://www.cancer.gov/about-cancer/treatment/cam/patient/mistletoe-pdq#section/_2 |title=Questions and Answers About Mistletoe |publisher=National Cancer Institute |access-date=3 December 2015 |date=24 March 2015}}{{cite journal |vauthors=Horneber MA, Bueschel G, Huber R, Linde K, Rostock M |title=Mistletoe therapy in oncology |journal=Cochrane Database Syst Rev |issue=2 |article-number=CD003297 |year=2008 |volume=2020 |pmid=18425885 |doi=10.1002/14651858.CD003297.pub2 |type=Systematic review|quote=The review found that there was not enough evidence to reach clear
